newsitem.title: CHINA: China jails 98 separatists in Tibet in 1996.
newsitem.headline: China jails 98 separatists in Tibet in 1996.

text.p: Chinese courts jailed nearly 100 Tibetan separatists last year, including a group who organised demonstrations, smashed up a police station and attacked officials, the Tibet Daily said.

Courts in the restive Himalayan region jailed 98 people last year for endangering national security, the June 3 edition of the newspaper -- available in Beijing on Thursday -- quoted Bai Zhao, president of the Tibet Higher People's Court, as saying. He gave no comparative figure.
The newspaper printed the full text of Bai's speech, which did not specify if any of the separatists were sentenced to death and executed.
In China, the maximum penalty for endangering national security is death.

Those convicted included "14 criminals who incited monks to shout anti-Beijing slogans, organised illegal demonstrations, smashed a police station, attacked government officials, stubbornly followed the Dalai Lama clique and tried in vain to split the motherland", the newspaper said.
"We resolutely punished in accordance with the law those criminal elements who endangered national security and engaged in splittist activities," Bai said.
The Intermediate People's Court in Lhasa, Tibet's capital, "ruthlessly dealt a blow to separatist elements swollen with arrogance", Bai said.

Beijing has come under fire from human rights groups and Western governments for its heavy-handed treatment of those seeking autonomy or independence for Tibet. Many monks and nuns are serving lengthy jail terms for expressing their views.
China dismisses such criticisms as interference in its internal affairs.
Tibet's chief prosecutor Tudengcaiwang said prosecutors and police should guard against "political, ideological and cultural infiltration of the Dalai Lama clique".
China has accused the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, of fomenting unrest in the region.
The Dalai Lama, who fled into exile in India in 1959 after an abortive uprising against communist rule, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his non-violent campaign for real autonomy for Tibet.

The deeply religious region of Tibet has been rocked in recent years by sporadic, sometimes violent, anti-Chinese unrest, with monks and nuns often at the forefront of demonstrations for independence.
The Tibet Daily said courts heard 2,126 criminal cases last year, up 31.23 percent from a year earlier.
Courts handed down verdicts in 1,853 of the cases, an increase of 20 percent compared with 1995, the newspaper said.
About 61 percent of convicted defendants were given sentences ranging from five years in prison to death, it said.
A total of 1,578 people were jailed for murder, robbery and rape as part of a government crackdown on crime.
"Our hands were certainly not soft with those who should be sentenced to death," Bai said, citing several convicted killers and robbers.
